question: The Financial Times, referring to information from EU officials, has reported that the EU intends to delay the strict enforcement of Regulation (EU) 2023/11151, which aims to reduce forest degradation caused by overconsumption in the EU and is an important part of the Green Deal. The decision follows complaints from Asian, African and Latin American governments who consider the new regulations and requirements to be very burdensome and unfair and are calling for more time to adapt2. 1.

Can the Commission confirm that, as a result of pressure from developing countries, the classification into low-, standard- and high-risk groups which was to have been implemented by December 2024 will be postponed and that a regional rather than a national breakdown will eventually be applied, and, if so, why is the Commission understanding of this and yielding to the demands of governments and farmers from third countries, while remaining steadfast against our farmers who are protesting against the Green Deal across the EU?

Does the Commission envisage a shortage on the EU market of goods covered by the EUDR as a result of the entry into force of the new requirements, such as determining the precise geolocation of production areas, which may be impossible to meet, especially for smaller farms in remote parts of the world?
Has the Commission carried out an assessment of the impact of implementing the EUDR on the prices of goods which are subject to it?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.7.2024) The Commission confirms that work on the benchmarking is underway, including on developing a technically sound and scientific methodology. The Commission is focusing its efforts on preparing all relevant tools for a smooth implementation and is providing support to Member States and stakeholders (including farmers) in multiple ways (e.g.

providing clarification via upcoming Frequently Asked Questions and an upcoming Guidance document, setting up an EU digital database (the Information System), etc.) The Commission is aware of reports in the media pointing to possible supply shortages in some areas. The Commission is actively engaged with relevant stakeholders to facilitate implementation and ensure a smooth application of the rules.

The Commission’s legislative proposal for the EU Deforestation Regulation1 was based on an impact assessment2 and a fitness check of the EU rules in place against illegal logging, including the EU Timber Regulation3. The potential impact on the prices of the seven commodities covered is expected to be limited.

This is based on the previous regulatory experience on wood (EU Timber Regulation) and the 31 December 2020 cut-off date that ensures that the vast majority of current agricultural production will be considered deforestation-free under the Regulation.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making

available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation and repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010, OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p. 206–247. 2 https://environment.ec.europa.

eu/publications/proposal-regulation-deforestation-free-products_en 3 Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 October 2010 laying down the obligations of operators who place timber and timber products on the market, OJ L 295, 12.11.2010, p. 23– 34.
